CHAPTER LXXXIV

THE HEARTH

The next day, Sunday, after mass, was a bustling day at Catherine's
house in the Hoog Straet. The shop was now quite ready, and Cornelis and
Sybrandt were to open it next day; their names were above the door; also
their sign, a white lamb sucking a gilt sheep. Eli had come, and brought
them some more goods from his store to give them a good start. The
hearts of the parents glowed at what they were doing, and the pair
themselves walked in the garden together, and agreed they were sick of
their old life, and it was more pleasant to make money than waste it;
they vowed to stick to business like wax. Their mother's quick and ever
watchful ear overheard this resolution through an open window, and she
told Eli, The family supper was to include Margaret and her boy, and be
a kind of inaugural feast, at which good trade advice was to flow from
the elders, and good wine to be drunk to the success of the converts
to Commerce from Agriculture in its unremunerative form--wild oats. So
Margaret had come over to help her mother-in-law, and also to shake
off her own deep languor; and both their faces were as red as the fire.
Presently in came Joan with a salad from Jorian's garden.

“He cut it for you, Margaret; you are all his chat; I shall be jealous.
I told him you were to feast to-day. But oh, lass, what a sermon in the
new kerk! Preaching? I never heard it till this day.”

“Would I had been there then,” said Margaret; “for I am dried up for
want of dew from heaven.”

“Why, he preacheth again this afternoon. But mayhap you are wanted
here.”

“Not she,” said Catherine. “Come, away ye go, if y'are minded.”

“Indeed,” said Margaret, “methinks I should not be such a damper at
table if I could come to 't warm from a good sermon.”

“Then you must be brisk,” observed Joan. “See the folk are wending that
way, and as I live, there goes the holy friar. Oh, bless us and save us,
Margaret; the hermit! We forgot.” And this active woman bounded out of
the house, and ran across the road, and stopped the friar. She returned
as quickly. “There, I was bent on seeing him nigh hand.”

“What said he to thee?”

“Says he, 'My daughter, I will go to him ere sunset, God willing.' The
sweetest voice. But oh, my mistresses, what thin cheeks for a young man,
and great eyes, not far from your colour, Margaret.”

“I have a great mind to go hear him,” said Margaret. “But my cap is not
very clean, and they will all be there in their snow-white mutches.”

“There, take my handkerchief out of the basket,” said Catherine; “you
cannot have the child, I want him for my poor Kate. It is one of her ill
days.”

Margaret replied by taking the boy upstairs. She found Kate in bed.

“How art thou, sweetheart? Nay, I need not ask. Thou art in sore pain;
thou smilest so, See,' I have brought thee one thou lovest.”

“Two, by my way of counting,” said Kate, with an angelic smile. She had
a spasm at that moment would have made some of us roar like bulls.

“What, in your lap?” said Margaret, answering a gesture of the suffering
girl. “Nay, he is too heavy, and thou in such pain.”

“I love him too dear to feel his weight,” was the reply.

Margaret took this opportunity, and made her toilet. “I am for the
kerk,” said she, “to hear a beautiful preacher.” Kate sighed. “And a
minute ago, Kate, I was all agog to go; that is the way with me this
month past; up and down, up and down, like the waves of the Zuyder Zee.
I'd as lieve stay aside thee; say the word!”

“Nay,” said Kate, “prithee go; and bring me back every word. Well-a-day
that I cannot go myself.” And the tears stood in the patient's eyes.
This decided Margaret, and she kissed Kate, looked under her lashes at
the boy, and heaved a little sigh. “I trow I must not,” said she. “I
never could kiss him a little; and my father was dead against waking
a child by day or night When 'tis thy pleasure to wake, speak thy aunt
Kate the two new words thou hast gotten.” And she went out, looking
lovingly over her shoulder, and shut the door inaudibly.


“Joan, you will lend me a hand, and peel these?” said Catherine.

“That I will, dame.” And the cooking proceeded with silent vigour.

“Now, Joan, them which help me cook and serve the meat, they help me eat
it; that's a rule.”

“There's worse laws in Holland than that. Your will is my pleasure,
mistress; for my Luke hath got his supper i' the air. He is digging
to-day by good luck.” (Margaret came down.)

“Eh, woman, yon is an ugly trade. There she has just washed her face
and gi'en her hair a turn, and now who is like her? Rotterdam, that for
you!” and Catherine snapped her fingers at the capital. “Give us a buss,
hussy! Now mind, Eli won't wait supper for the duke. Wherefore, loiter
not after your kerk is over.”

Joan and she both followed her to the door, and stood at it watching
her a good way down the street. For among homely housewives going out
o' doors is half an incident. Catherine commented on the launch: “There,
Joan, it is almost to me as if I had just started my own daughter for
kerk, and stood a looking after: the which I've done it manys and manys
the times. Joan, lass, she won't hear a word against our Gerard; and
he be alive, he has used her cruel; that is why my bowels yearn for the
poor wench. I'm older and wiser than she; and so I'll wed her to yon
simple Luke, and there an end. What's one grandchild?”

[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.

Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

The following day, a Sunday consecrated to commerce rather than contemplation, transformed Catherine's dwelling in the Hoog Straet into a hive of industrious anticipation. The shop stood unveiled and fully prepared, a testament to the relentless energy of Cornelis and Sybrandt, whose names were already etched above the threshold alongside their heraldic emblem: a white lamb suckling a gilded sheep. Eli had arrived bearing fresh provisions from his store, eager to fortify their enterprise before the official opening. Within the domestic sphere, the atmosphere shimmered with a feverish optimism; the parents' hearts burned with the heat of reinvention. They strolled through the garden, their steps synchronized by a shared resolve to abandon the drudgery of their agrarian past. "We are weary of the soil," Sybrandt declared, his voice ringing with the clarity of conversion. "It is far sweeter to mint coin than to squander it upon wild oats. Let us bind ourselves to business as tightly as wax to the seal."

Catherine's mother, her ears perpetually attuned to the currents of household fortune, intercepted this vow through an open lattice. She relayed the news to Eli: the evening supper would serve as an inaugural banquet, welcoming Margaret and her son. It was to be a rite of passage where seasoned merchants would dispense wisdom upon the converts fleeing the unremunerative fields of agriculture, and where vintage wine would toast the triumph of commerce over the earth. Margaret descended to assist her mother-in-law, driven by a dual necessity to aid the household and to shed the heavy languor that had settled upon her spirit. Both women emerged flushed, their complexions glowing with the vibrant red of embers, signaling a vitality long dormant.

Suddenly, the front door swung open, admitting Joan carrying a crisp salad harvested from Jorian's garden. "He cut it specifically for you, Margaret," Joan announced, her tone laced with playful rivalry. "You are his sole conversation; I fear I shall become jealous. I reminded him of today's feast, but alas, what a thunderous sermon echoed from the new church! Preaching? I have never witnessed such a spectacle until this hour."

"I wish I had been present," Margaret murmured, her voice tinged with a spiritual thirst. "I am parched, deprived of the dew from heaven."

"Why, he preaches again this afternoon," Joan countered, her eyes darting toward the street. "Yet, perhaps your duties demand you remain here."

"Not she," Catherine interjected firmly. "Go, if your heart inclines you."

"Indeed," Margaret hesitated, "but methinks I should not dampen the spirits at the table if I could attend, warmed by the fervor of a divine discourse."

"Then you must move with alacrity," Joan advised, scanning the horizon. "Observe the congregation gathering; look, even the holy friar approaches. Oh, blessed be our salvation, Margaret—the hermit! We have forgotten him entirely." With a burst of kinetic energy, the active woman launched herself from the doorway, crossed the cobblestones, and halted the friar mid-stride. She returned moments later, breathless. "Behold, I was determined to view him in person."

"What did he impart to thee?"

"He spoke thus: 'My daughter, I shall visit him ere sunset, God willing,'" Joan recounted, her voice softening. "His voice was the sweetest melody. Yet, oh, my mistresses, observe his gaunt cheeks, those hollow features of a young man, and his great eyes, remarkably akin to yours, Margaret."

"I possess a strong desire to hear him," Margaret confessed. "However, my cap lacks cleanliness, and the assembly will surely wear their pristine white mutches."

"There," Catherine instructed, reaching into a woven basket, "take my handkerchief. I cannot spare the child; I require him for my poor Kate, who suffers from one of her grievous days."

Margaret ascended the stairs, leaving the boy behind. She found Kate confined to bed, her body wracked with agony. "How fares thou, sweetheart?" Margaret asked gently. "No inquiry is necessary; thou art in profound pain. Yet, thou smilest. Behold, I have brought thee one thou lovest."

"Two, by my reckoning," Kate replied, her countenance radiant with an angelic serenity despite the torment. Suddenly, a violent spasm seized her, a convulsion that might have caused onlookers to roar like bulls in their distress.

"In your lap?" Margaret queried, responding to the suffering girl's gesture.

"Nay, he is too heavy, and thou art in such anguish," Kate protested weakly.

"I love him too dearly to feel his weight," was the tender rebuttal. Seizing this brief respite, Margaret attended to her own preparations.

"I am bound for the church," she announced, "to listen to a magnificent preacher."

Kate sighed, a sound of resigned longing. "A moment ago, I was eager to depart; such is my condition for the past month. Up and down, up and down, like the restless waves of the Zuyder Zee. I would sooner remain beside thee; simply say the word!"

"Nay," Kate pleaded, her eyes filling with tears. "Pray, go. Bring me back every syllable. Alas, that I cannot journey myself."

This plea resolved Margaret's hesitation. She kissed Kate, glanced beneath her eyelashes at the sleeping infant, and let out a small, sorrowful sigh. "I deem I must not," she whispered. "I could never bear to kiss him lightly; nor could my father endure waking a child by day or night. Speak to Aunt Kate the two new words thou hast acquired when it is thy pleasure to rise." With a final, loving glance over her shoulder, she departed, shutting the door with an inaudible click.

Downstairs, Catherine turned to Joan. "Will you lend me a hand to peel these vegetables?"

"That I will, dame," Joan responded promptly.

Cooking resumed with a silent, vigorous intensity. "Listen well, Joan," Catherine commanded, chopping rhythmically. "Those who assist me in preparing and serving the meat shall share in eating it; that is the law of our house."

"There exist harsher statutes in Holland than that," Joan retorted cheerfully. "Your will is my delight, mistress. My Luke awaits his supper in the air; fortunately, he is digging today."

Margaret descended the stairs. "Eh, woman, that is a grim trade indeed."

She had merely washed her face and arranged her hair, and suddenly, she appeared transformed. "Rotterdam, that for you!" Catherine exclaimed, snapping her fingers in admiration of the capital city's influence on beauty. "Give us a buss, hussy! Mind now, Eli will not wait for the Duke to join us. Loiter not after your church service concludes."

Joan and Catherine accompanied Margaret to the threshold, standing sentinel as she ventured down the street. Among the mundane routines of housewives, the act of departing home holds half the drama of any event. Catherine paused to comment on the procession. "There, Joan, it feels as though I had just dispatched my own daughter to church, standing guard to ensure her safety—a vigilance I have performed countless times. Joan, lass, she will not tolerate a single word spoken against our Gerard. If he remains alive, he has treated her cruelly; hence, my bowels ache for the poor wretch. Being older and wiser, I intend to wed her to that simple Luke, and there shall be an end to her suffering. What is one grandchild more?"
